newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi lawyer to seek clemency for British nurses.
newsitem.headline: Saudi lawyer to seek clemency for British nurses.

text.p: A lawyer for two British nurses charged with murder in Saudi Arabia said in remarks published on Wednesday he would seek clemency from the victim's family after he receives the final police report.

Saudi lawyer Salah al-Hejailan has already received the forensic medical report on the killing of Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford, 55, at a hospital complex in the country's Eastern Province in December.

Both reports are considered key elements in the case and could pave the way for the trial of Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, who have been charged with the murder and could face public beheading by the sword if convicted.
Gilford's family in Australia has ruled out a clemency appeal, saying the two should face the maximum punishment.
Legal sources say it would be the first time Western women had been beheaded in the conservative Islamic kingdom.

"I hope that the victim's family will change their mind about not granting the clemency to my clients in light of the truths which will be revealed about the case, after both the forensic report and the final police report," the Arab News daily quoted Hejailan as saying.
He said he expected to call them some time in mid-February after Eid al-Fitr, the feast marking the end of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.
Legal experts said that if they were found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder the nurses would not be condemned to death.
Gilford was found murdered in her dormitory room at the King Fahd military medical complex in the oil city of Dhahran on December 11. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.

In accordance with Saudi law, there will be no prosecution lawyer at the trial, only the police report with a judge handling the rest of the prosecution case. No date for the hearing has been announced.
If found guilty and sentenced to death, Gilford's family could still spare the lives of the women by accepting financial recompense, known as blood money, instead of execution.

Hejailan said two leading British lawyers, Peter Watson and Paul Bonano, former head of the British Law Association, were expected to visit Saudi Arabia next month to cooperate with him on a "technical level" and to visit the defendants in jail.
Saudi police said the nurses confessed to the murder and the confession had been filed with three judges.
But Hejailan's law firm said the women had withdrawn their confessions, and one of them retracted a statement that she had a lesbian relationship with the victim.
